#2718. 5 final observations for the 49ers following Raiders win and trade deadline

The San Francisco 49ers are coming off an eventful few days following their 38-17 win over the Las Vegas Raiders and the trade deadline, where the team added Indianapolis Colts wide receiver Keenan Allen after trading for DeForest Buckner last week.

Now, the 49ers are set for the second half of the season with two new veterans in the fold, as they await several injury updates for this weekend's game against the Dallas Cowboys.

San Francisco was still banged up offensively against the Raiders, playing without Deebo Samuel and Mike Evans, but they still put up 38 points. Meanwhile, the defense continued to shine, creating five turnovers that sealed the deal for the Raiders.

Here are five observations from after the trade deadline following the Raiders win.

We've heard Kyle Shanahan talk about 'trust' when referencing Jordan Watkins, and we really saw that come out this past weekend, as the second-year wideout had his best game with four catches for 86 yards and a touchdown.

Watkins has paced the 49ers wide receivers in snaps with Mike Evans out, leading the team in the Washington, Atlanta, and Las Vegas games. That wasn't the case before that, though, as Watkins had been behind Brandin Cooks and Jacob Cowing in addition to San Francisco's top receivers in the weeks prior.

But now, post trade deadline, it feels like he could be in the top group for the 49ers until Mike Evans returns, joining Keenan Allen and Deebo Samuel. With this group of receivers, Watkins and Demarcus Robinson can play the vertical role, which means they're live for big plays every week.

We saw one of those come down last weekend with Watkins's 37-yard touchdown grab. On the season, he's now averaging 22.6 yards per catch. That trust is finally starting to pay off.

The 49ers have made it a goal to get Jaden Dugger on the field in a variety of roles this year. Dugger played 12 defensive snaps against Las Vegas, with only three coming in the box. 5 came on the line of scrimmage, while four were in the slot.

He's been a tackling machine, but also got a pick-six this past weekend. There were initial questions on usage for Dugger coming into the NFL as a Day 3 rookie, but he's been a fit everywhere.

Against Atlanta, Dugger played 31 snaps, with a ton coming on the line of scrimmage. With Dre Greenlaw out against Washington, he was much more of a full-time linebacker. Back in Week 5, he played 47 defensive snaps, with 16 being in the slot or on the line.

The snap count might dwindle with Upton Stout getting fully healthy and less need in the nickel, but Dugger has been a pleasant surprise so far this year in his usage.

DeForest Buckner was welcomed to the Bay Area and instantly played the most snaps of any defensive tackle against Las Vegas. He was on the field for 34 of the 50 defensive snaps, recording two pressures while Osa Odighizuwa had three.

Buckner was one of the most-played linemen in the NFL in Indianapolis, ranking in the top five in snap count. The 49ers will look to rotate him more than Indianapolis did, but it's clear he's going to have a big role, and the need was only further exacerbated by Gracen Halton's injury.

The 49ers seemed pretty adamant on adding a wide receiver, and even in his current state, Keenan Allen seems to fit what the team wants with his separation and blocking skills.

But with him in the fold, the future of the 49ers wide receiver room this season got more interesting. San Francisco seems to be getting Deebo Samuel back this weekend. They also should get Mike Evans in the coming weeks, while De'Zhaun Stribling is expected back in the regular season.

Then, there's Demarcus Robinson and the emerging Jordan Watkins alongside punt returner Jacob Cowing.

The first question comes with the starting group. When Evans, and really Stribling is back, will the 49ers rely on Allen still? And then, who is the odd man out of the group?

San Francisco will have Allen, Evans, Samuel, Stribling, Robinson, Watkins, and Cowing as their receivers then. They likely don't dress seven guys. Cowing has not been good as a receiver, but has maintained the punt return job. Does that go elsewhere and he's the odd man out? Or will the 49ers make a different move?

A lot of the 49ers focus on offense has been about the passing game, with Brock Purdy enjoying a career year and Mike Evans shining in his first season in the Bay.

But the 49ers run game has sneakily been elite this year from an efficiency perspective. The 49ers are seventh in yards per game (135.3) and seventh in yards per attempt (4.6). They're also third in EPA per rush and first in rushing success rate, so they've really turned things around in the run game.

San Francisco has adapted to the two-headed monster with Christian McCaffrey and Kaelon Black, whose efficiency has risen in recent weeks. The offensive line has done a good job overall, and the Niners are quite balanced offensively.

That's a big sign for the coming weeks as the passing game still works through injuries, with the 49ers having their hardest stretch of the schedule coming up.

The Rams have experienced a bevy of injuries so far this season.

One consequence of that is the team’s slots for players to return from injured reserve are getting fewer and fewer.

Shesterkin suffered an apparent leg injury in the Rangers' loss to the Washington Capitals on Friday night as his right leg slid awkwardly into the post while scrambling to get back in position. Shesterkin fell to the ice immediately, and he needed assistance to get down the tunnel.

Prior to that loss, the Rangers were off to a terrific 4-1-0 start, and Shesterkin was a driving force behind that success. In just five appearances, Shesterkin posted 3.90 goals saved above average with a .900 high-danger save percentage, according to Natural Stat Trick.

The 2022 Vezina Trophy winner, Shesterkin has put up sparkling numbers since he entered the NHL in 2019-20. In 330 games, Shesterkin boasts a .917 save percentage, a 2.51 GAA and 22 shutouts. Over the last three full seasons from 2023-26, Shesterkin ranked third in goals saved above average with 45.4. Only Connor Hellebuyck and Andrei Vasilevskiy were better in that category.

Shesterkin was a big reason why the Rangers felt they could bounce back from a disappointing 2025-26 season, and losing the star goaltender puts a huge dent in the team's playoff hopes. It doesn't help that backup goalie Joonas Korpisalo is also hurt.

Dylan Garand replaced Shesterkin on Friday night, and Spencer Martin will be recalled from the AHL after recovering from his own injury. With the Rangers playing well early, it wouldn't be a shock to see them explore better replacement options for Shesterkin.

New York won't be able to replace Shesterkin's impact because he's one of the five best goalies in the world. However, the team should be able to upgrade its current goaltending situation, which is a fairly low bar to clear.

First, there are unsigned veterans still on the open market in Petr Mrazek and James Reimer. Neither one was great last season -- hence their availability at the moment -- Reimer and Mrazek could provide a level of stability in the crease that the Rangers simply don't have right now.

New York could also explore trade possibilities, and Minnesota Wild netminder Filip Gustavsson could be a solution there. Jesper Wallstedt is the future of the crease in Minnesota, making Gustavsson more of a luxury. Would the Wild send Gustavsson to New York in exchange for some draft capital it could use to acquire a center?

The one snag in a potential Gustavsson deal is his contract. Gustavsson is in the first year of a deal that pays him $6.8 million over the next five seasons. That's a big commitment for a player who will become a backup when Shesterkin returns.

Obviously, Connor Hellebuyck has been on the trade market for months now, but that trade wouldn't make sense for the Rangers. Hellebuyck is on an expensive long-term deal, and New York would have $20 million tied up in goalies if they made that move, not to mention the astronomical acquisition cost.

However, if you'll allow me to get creative here, it's no secret that the Florida Panthers have pursed Hellebuyck. What if the Panthers traded Jacob Markstrom -- just acquired in the offseason -- to the Rangers in order to make room for Hellebuyck?

Markstrom does have a 20-team no-trade list, so the question is whether New York would be one of his 11 approved teams. Florida flipping Markstrom so quickly seems like a long shot, but the team has taken plenty of big swings in recent history.

#2711. Winners and losers from Ravens’ Week 9 loss to the Jaguars

The Baltimore Ravens' 33-10 loss to the Jacksonville Jaguars was their third consecutive game decided by at least 22 points. There was more bad than good in this one for the Ravens, as you would expect in such a lopsided contest.

RB Justice Hill: Hill was one of the few bright spots for Baltimore on Thursday night. The seventh-year veteran showed he still had burst on a 65-yard touchdown run in the fourth quarter. Hill's 85 rushing yards were the most allowed to a single player by the Jaguars in their last 24 games.

C Cam Jurgens: Jurgens rebounded from a poor game last week with a solid outing against Jacksonville. His 72.7 PFF grade was the highest of any offensive player for the Ravens.

RG Vega Ioane: Ioane's return to the lineup after missing the previous game with a knee injury was a welcome sight. The rookie's 66.7 PFF grade was only behind Jurgens among offensive players.

RT Roger Rosengarten: Rosengarten allowed zero pressures against the Jaguars and was third among offensive players with a 66.4 PFF grade.

QB Joe Fagnano: The rookie undrafted quarterback making his first start on a short week with an injured ankle played how you would expect. Fagnano struggled to move the ball through the air, racking up just 60 yards on 18 attempts, while throwing two interceptions.

LG John Simpson: Simpson has been perhaps the most criticized starter on Baltimore's offensive line after signing a three-year, $30 million contract this offseason. His 4.5 pass-blocking grade against Jacksonville should only stoke the flames.

TE Mark Andrews: Highly-paid veterans continue to let the Ravens down this season, and no player exemplifies that more than their once Pro Bowl tight end. Andrews and Ronnie Stanley appear to be in competition at this point for who can have the most false starts, as the duo committed the penalty on consecutive plays to move the ball back 10 yards on second down. Andrews later fumbled the handoff on a fourth down, turning the ball over on downs.

CB Marlon Humphrey: Humphrey continues to draw the ire of fans with comments made off the field, and his play on it only strengthens the criticism. Humphrey allowed a 52-yard completion to a tight end on the game's opening drive when he appeared to get stuck watching Trevor Lawrence on a scramble, allowing the rookie Nate Boerkircher to get behind him down the field.

WR LaJohntay Wester: Wester has failed to make much of an impact in the return game this season, and his lost fumble on a kickoff against the Jaguars could put his job security in question.

#2709. Lauri Markkanen injury update could have major fallout for Utah Jazz

The Utah Jazz hoped to be part of the Western Conference playoff race this season after years of rebuilding. But those plans have gone horribly awry during the opening few weeks of the 2026-27 NBA campaign, and getting back on track just became even more difficult after a sobering update involving star Lauri Markkanen.

Markkanen is expected to miss at least a month of action, the Jazz announced on Nov. 11, after suffering a right hand injury during the team's loss to the Dallas Mavericks last Friday. Markkanen is the latest key Jazz player to be sidelined, and the mounting absences have left Utah tied for the NBA's worst record at 1-10 entering Wednesday's matchup against the Orlando Magic.

Here's more on Markkanen's injury status and what it means for the Jazz's hopes of reaching the postseason.

NBA: Kon Knueppel's latest injury setback could be crushing blow for Hornets

Markkanen has been diagnosed with two nondisplaced fractures in his right hand and will be re-evaluated in four weeks. The good news is a nondisplaced fracture is considered less severe than a displaced fracture, in which the bones are no longer in proper alignment. A non-displaced fracture generally doesn't require surgery.

The 29-year-old forward had already been playing through a sprained right wrist as the Jazz were hit hard with injuries during the first month of the NBA season. An initial X-ray did not reveal the fracture, according to ESPN, but Markkanen underwent scans that revealed more damage after returning to Utah in recent days.

The Jazz were already teetering to start the 2026-27 season because of injuries, and they've lost 10 of their first 11 games. Utah watched Jaren Jackson Jr. go down for at least two months with a knee injury, while center Jusuf Nurkic has yet to appear in a game this season because of a toe injury. Guard Keyonte George has also been dealing with a sprained ankle and did not play in Tuesday's loss to the Miami Heat.

That leaves rookie Darryn Peterson as the only player from the Jazz's expected Opening Night starting lineup currently available entering Wednesday.

Utah was already struggling with Markkanen in the lineup, and losing its most reliable offensive weapon only makes an uphill climb steeper. His ability to score at all three levels, stretch defenses and create matchup problems is central to everything the Jazz want to do offensively. The timing is just brutal. A team that entered the season hoping to take a step forward is suddenly staring at the possibility of another year buried near the bottom of the Western Conference.

The injury could also create bigger-picture questions for the franchise. The Jazz resisted opportunities to trade Markkanen when his value was arguably at its peak, believing he would be the centerpiece of their return to contention. Now, with Utah off to a disastrous start and its roster ravaged by injuries, the mission is simply to keep the season from slipping away before Markkanen can return.

If this season ends as disastrously as it has started, the Jazz could revisit assumptions that have guided their moves to this point, including whether their current timeline and roster construction around Markkanen remain the right path forward.

Markkanen was averaging 18 points and 6.8 rebounds per game through eight games for the Jazz this season. He was shooting just 38.9% from the floor, which is the worst mark of his career. Markkanen averaged 26.7 points on 47.7% shooting during the 2025-26 season.

#2708. Kevin O'Connell on Kyler Murray: I want him to get healthy, you never know what could happen

The Vikings made Kyler Murray their quarterback choice to open the 2026 season, but it didn’t take long for their plans to go awry.

Murray was concussed early in the season opener, missed Week 2 and then led an underwhelming offense to a 4-1 record before suffering a hamstring injury in Week 8. The Vikings offense got even worse with Carson Wentz in Monday night’s loss to the Bills, which led the team to trade for Kirk Cousins on Tuesday.

Head coach Kevin O’Connell hasn’t committed to starting Cousins against the Packers this weekend, but it’s why the deal was made and Murray isn’t currently an option because he remained out of practice with a hamstring injury on Wednesday. Once Murray is healthy, he’ll be slated for a backup role as O’Connell said he doesn’t believe “you can have a competition during the season” and that his hope is that Murray is available if and when the Vikings have to pivot again.

“The reality is what it is,” O’Connell said. “It’s one of those things where I think he appreciated hearing about it before the transaction took place, but at the same time, he knows I believe in him. I believe in Kyler, just like I believe in Carson and I believe in Max [Brosmer]. I want him to get healthy and get back to work because you just never know. We do not hold the cards in how this will go from a health standpoint or anything like that with anybody on our team.”

O’Connell said that he told Murray that he knows it has been a “less than ideal” series of events, but that underscores the possibility that the Vikings will have to turn back to him with an important game on the line at some point later this year.

#2706. Bruno Senna reveals plans to put Kimi Antonelli behind the wheel of Ayrton Senna's F1 car

Former Formula 1 driver Bruno Senna says he wants to give Kimi Antonelli the chance to drive one of Ayrton Senna's cars next year, after the 2026 world champion visited the family's estate in Brazil.

Antonelli arrived at the estate days after clinching his maiden F1 championship at the Mexican Grand Prix, becoming the youngest driver in the history of the series to win the title.

Speaking on F1's Beyond The Grid podcast, Bruno said the Mercedes driver barely wanted to get out of the Lotus 98T that his uncle raced in 1986.

"It was really, really fun to see him," he said. "We have the Lotus, the '86 car. We had him jump inside the car, and he didn't want to leave the car. You had the turbo boost knob, and he's exploring everything – having an anti-roll bar thing that you can change, and there's a gearstick."

Antonelli's love of the Lotus 98T gave Bruno the idea of having the Italian drive the car next year.

"This is something that was quite funny – I was talking [about] next year when Lotus or McLaren want to do something, we can try to organise for [him] to drive one of these cars because he fits really well in the car," he continued.

"You know, his height is perfect for it. His dad was like, 'I'm not sure if you can drive the manual car', and Kimi was like, 'sure I can!'"

In addition to sitting in the Lotus 98T, Antonelli also had some time on the go-kart track that Ayrton designed on the estate, where Bruno saw first-hand what the 20-year-old can do.

"Finally, we drove on the go-kart track that Ayrton designed," he added. "It was a really fun thing when I was a kid, and Kimi was incredible. He was so fast, so consistent. We had a fun time. I would say that I was slower because I'm 10kg heavier, but I think there's a bit more than that in it, to be honest! He was amazing.

"The track was very dirty, very full of stone. Kimi was able to create a groove, and he was able to stay within that groove so consistently. It was really impressive. He couldn't move 10cm off because then you don't even run wide – you go onto the grass and spin out because it was so dirty. It was a really cool experience and showed why he's a world champion."

The Jacksonville Jaguars kicked off the NFL trade news cycle for the week with a splash move to bolster the secondary, sending a 2027 second-round pick and a 2028 fifth-round pick to the Atlanta Falcons in exchange for Pro Bowl safety Jessie Bates III. They continued adding on defense throughout the day, also acquiring Davon Godchaux from the New Orleans Saints and former first-round pick Jordan Davis in a blockbuster deal with the Philadelphia Eagles.

The Indianapolis Colts were another team to watch ahead of the trade deadline, with star running back Jonathan Taylor at the crux of it all. But as was first reported by NFL insider Tom Pelissero, the Colts did not trade Taylor ahead of Tuesday's deadline. The Colts did, however, trade wide receiver Josh Downs, who gets a fresh start with the Kansas City Chiefs and quarterback Patrick Mahomes.

Now, with all of that officially a wrap, it's time to gear up for Week 10.

Follow along with Yahoo Sports for the latest NFL news, injury updates and more ahead of Week 10.

After a great deal of speculation was made that Jonathan Taylor could be moved ahead of the NFL trade deadline, the Indianapolis Colts are reportedly standing pat.

The team will not trade him ahead of the deadline, NFL insider Tom Pelissero reported Tuesday afternoon.

Pelissero reported that the Colts had received multiple offers for Taylor of a second-round pick-plus, but instead, the team will move forward with him as a foundational piece within the locker room as they look to rebuild.

Riley Patterson will kick for the Ravens this week in their Monday Night Football matchup with the Chargers, according to the NFL Network's Mike Garafolo. Patterson spent the past two seasons with the Dolphins, but was released last month.

The Patriots will be playing the Lions in Munich, Germany, on Sunday.

Running back TreVeyon Henderson did not practice on Wednesday, and with an upcoming flight across the pond, the team has already ruled him out.

Henderson was listed on the injury report as dealing with an illness. The running back revealed last Friday that he recently experienced "an unexpected and unusual medical emergency involving a series of unexplained neurological symptoms." Henderson was hospitalized, but has said that test results have been positive and reassuring.

Starting running back Rhamondre Stevenson also didn't practice on Wednesday due to a knee injury, but has not yet been ruled out, though he is expected to miss a few weeks.

Sean McVay delivered a mix bag of news Wednesday regarding injuries to the team's top two receivers.

Davante Adams could be back sooner than expected from a hamstring injury, potentially in Week 13 vs. the Chiefs. Puka Nacua, meanwhile, will remain sidelined for a "significant period of time" with knee and toe injuries.

Etienne has been out since Week 3 due to a hamstring injury and has since been on injured reserve.

His return to practice opens his 21-day window to return to action, meaning the Saints have three weeks to activate him to the 53-man roster or shut him down for the season.

Skattebo missed Sunday's win over the Eagles coming out of the team's bye week. The running back practiced this week, which sets him up for a return Thursday night against the Commanders.

McCarthy was sacked five times in the game and suffered a rib injury that briefly took him out of action. He would return and finished 12-for-19 for 127 yards passing.

"I feel really good," McCarthy said this week. "Obviously, Sunday, it's football, it's a physical game, but just credit to the athletic training staff, getting me back to feeling really good as quick as possible."

The 49ers acquired Keenan Allen ahead of Tuesday's trade deadline because of the various injuries the team has at the position.

San Francisco head coach Kyle Shanahan said on Wednesday that Mike Evans remains week-to-week due to an Achilles injury. At this point, he has not been added to IR, so Evans could suit up this week against the Cowboys, but he is starting the week by not practicing.

Shanahan added that currently there is no timeline for Evans' return.

The Rams are expected to be without star wide receiver Puka Nacua for more than a month after suffering two knee sprains in the team's most recent game.

Nacua, who would normally be added to IR to free up a roster spot, won't be, according to head coach Sean McVay. L.A. is still expecting Nacua to miss extended time, but NFL teams are only allowed eight player activations from IR per season.

If Nacua gets added, with the intention of activating him in December, he would take up an activation from another player that the Rams were planning on activating, which would rule them out for the year.

L.A. currently has WR Davante Adams, G Justin Dedich, DT Poona Ford and DE Kobie Turner on IR and the Rams likely want to be able to activate all of them later this year. Los Angeles has already used four activations with EDGE Myles Garrett, TE Terrance Ferguson, OT Keagan Trost and RB Ronnie Rivers.

The 49ers acquired Keenan Allen ahead of Tuesday's trade deadline to help bolster the banged-up wide receiver room.

The only problem is that Allen could still miss time this season. Kyle Shanahan acknowledged to reporters on Wednesday that the veteran wideout could still face league discipline this season stemming from his DUI in August.

According to the current CBA, a violation of the league's substance-abuse policy, which would include a DUI, comes with a minimum three-game suspension. Additionally, Allen's BAC was so high that the league can increase the suspension if it so chooses.

The league has reportedly been waiting for the DUI case against Allen to play out legally before issuing the suspension.

Pittsburgh is allowing the seventh-fewest yards per game and the third-fewest rush yards per game this season.

Brown has missed the Patriots' last two games due to a knee injury. The wide receiver has only played in three games for New England this season, as he missed the early part of the season because of a sprained ankle in Week 1.

The wide receiver has caught nine of his 20 targets for 101 yards. Brown has yet to score a touchdown this year.

Tuesday's trade deadline was highlighted by the return of quarterback Kirk Cousins to the Minnesota Vikings.

Despite the move, on Wednesday, Minnesota head coach Kevin O'Connell wasn't ready to commit to Cousins as the starter this weekend against the Packers.

This could just be gamesmanship by O'Connell, but he told the media about Cousins starting: "I will say [we're] excited about the opportunity of spending every moment we can between now and then to get him comfortable and allow him to play for us this Sunday. Green Bay head coach Matt LaFleur said in his Wednesday press conference that he was surprised that the Raiders didn't get more for Cousins. "I was surprised [the Raiders] didn't get more for him, quite honestly. I was shocked when I saw what they traded him for."

Green Bay Packers running back Josh Jacobs may not end up on injured reserve despite needing surgery on his broken ring finger.

Jacobs, who is set to have that procedure later this week, could be back as soon as 2-3 weeks, according to NFL Network's Ian Rapoport, who also reported that Green Bay will decide Saturday if IR is necessary.

The Packers play the Minnesota Vikings on Sunday. But then they have a bye. There's a chance Jacobs returns for the following week's road game against the Los Angeles Rams.

The Chiefs will stick with Harrison Butker in Week 10, giving the kicker another chance to turn things around after weeks of struggles, head coach Andy Reid announced Wednesday.

After Sunday's win over the Jets, in which Butker missed another field goal attempt (a 51-yarder), Reid said that he would "look at everything" to assess whether it was time to move on. Evidently, Reid decided to stick with his long-time kicker.

Butker, who has spent his entire 10-year NFL career with the Chiefs, has seen his field goal accuracy crater this season. He's missed seven field goals in eight games so far this year, going 12-of-19 on attempts. That 63% completion rate is a noticeable dip from his previous decade of experience.

New York Jets wide receiver Garrett Wilson will be back at practice Wednesday, albeit in a limited capacity while coming off a concussion, per ESPN's Rich Cimini.

Wilson was sidelined during last week's 35-12 road loss to the Kansas City Chiefs.

He absorbed a blow to the head from safety Jeremy Chinn late in a Week 8 defeat to the Las Vegas Raiders. Wilson then reported concussion symptoms the following Monday, Jets head coach Aaron Glenn told reporters.

Wilson has piled up 43 receptions, 527 receiving yards and 3 receiving touchdowns this season.

The Cleveland Browns are expected to turn back to quarterback Deshaun Watson in Week 10, according to The Athletic.

Browns head coach Todd Monken shot down those rumors Monday, however, saying he had yet to make a decision on the team's starter in Week 10.

With backup running back Tyler Goodson sidelined with a knee sprain, Miller adds a potential depth piece behind starter Javonte Williams.

Acquiring Kirk Cousins wasn't the only notable Vikings roster move on Tuesday.

Baltimore sent G Andrew Vorhees and a 2028 6th-round pick to Atlanta for C Ryan Neuzil, per The Athletic's Jonathan Jones.

Darius Acuff Jr. is not happy, and it's easy to understand why.

The Sacramento Kings rookie, after the team fell to just 1-10 on the new season with a loss to the Orlando Magic on Tuesday night, is starting to feel the frustrations that come with having one of the worst records in the NBA.

"I'm not a loser, so it's not fun," Acuff said, via ESPN. "But like I said, it's an 82-game season, so hopefully something will stick."

Acuff finished with 29 points in Tuesday's 107-100 loss to the Magic. He shot 10 of 21 from the field, and had six assists and four rebounds to go with it.

Acuff has been having an impressive rookie campaign so far. The 19-year-old, who the Kings selected with the No. 7 overall pick out of Arkansas this past summer, has averaged 26.2 points and 7.3 assists per game this season — both of which are among the top 12 throughout the league. He matched the NBA's single-game rookie 3-point record when he drained nine of them in a loss to the Memphis Grizzlies last month, which was also the most ever made in a contest by a teenager.

He's also racked up 288 points through the team's first 11 games of the season, which is the most by a rookie over that span since Michael Jordan's first season in the league in 1984. Jordan had 289 points through his first 11 games.

Despite all of that, the Kings aren't winning. They are 0-6 at the Golden 1 Center, and their lone win came on the road against the Dallas Mavericks. They've lost four straight entering Friday's contest against the Portland Trail Blazers.

The Kings are currently tied for the worst record in the NBA with the Utah Jazz and Milwaukee Bucks. The Chicago Bulls are also equal in the win column at 1-8.

Even though Acuff may be mounting a solid Rookie of the Year campaign, it certainly doesn't feel like things are going well in Sacramento just yet.

"I don't know what to do," Acuff said. "I feel like we're trying, everybody as a whole. We're just not coming out with the win.

#2699. Phoenix Suns Will Continue Building Around Devin Booker After 11 Years

As it stands, the Phoenix Suns have yet to prove themselves as a Western Conference contender. After going 45-37 in 2025-26, they had ambitions of taking a step up in the Western Conference, only to start 4-6 this season.

As the Suns continue to struggle, star shooting guard Devin Booker's future has been questioned, sparking countless rumors across the NBA. This week, however, league insider Michael Scotto provided the latest intel on the Suns, confirming their commitment to build around Booker for the foreseeable future.

"From every indication I've gotten, the Phoenix Suns want to keep Devin Booker, and they want to make the team better around him," said Michael Scotto. "From Devin Booker, every indication I've gotten is that he still wants to be a Sun for life, ideally. He did an extension recently with them, and he's been the face of the franchise for a while now. For Phoenix right now, it's about trying to make the team better around him."

In the era of player empowerment, NBA teams have to try harder than ever to keep their stars, and the Suns are no exception. Since drafting shooting guard Devin Booker in 2015, they've tried to build around him, with varying degrees of success. As recently as 2021, they made the NBA Finals, but the Suns have been unable to replicate that formula after losing key stars like Kevin Durant and Bradley Beal.

This season, despite celebrated summer signings, the Suns are struggling to keep up with the top contenders. At 4-6, they are 11th in the Western Conference and considered underdogs to advance to the NBA playoffs. Despite this, the Suns remain committed to building around Booker, their leading star since 2015.

Drafted 13th overall, Booker has been the face of the Suns for years now, outlasting several star teammates, including Chris Paul and Kevin Durant. This season, through the first 10 games, Booker is averaging 25.1 points, 2.7 rebounds, 4.8 assists, and 1.0 steals on 48.3% shooting from the field. With those stats, Devin would net a valuable return in a trade, but the Suns aren't ready to test the market, despite being 4-6.

With team owner Mat Ishbia committed to immediate results, the Suns are more likely to make a win-now move around Booker than to trade him and start from scratch. Drafted 13th overall in 2015, Booker has been a reliable scorer for the Suns, averaging 24.6 points, 4.0 rebounds, 5.3 assists, 1.0 steal, and 0.3 blocks per game on 48.3% shooting.

The problem is, Phoenix has yet to meet expectations in the Booker era. Despite trying to stack the deck in their favor, the Suns have seen a sharp decline in the West, raising questions about Booker's future. But with both the Suns and Booker himself set on continuing their partnership, there's no question about what comes next for this team. At 11th in the West, the Suns are scrambling to improve their standing and keep Booker satisfied, but only time will tell how it pays off. At the very least, rival teams should know the Suns aren't ready to blow it up and trade all their best assets before February's deadline.

One of the biggest benefits of the NIL era is that college basketball has more elite talent than ever, now that players are returning for bigger paychecks instead of bolting for NBA money at the first opportunity.

That made selecting our 2026-27 CBS Sports Preseason All-America teams especially difficult, but our experts nailed it. Each of the three teams features players who will be performing at the next level very soon, but the best of those might be Florida superstar Thomas Haugh.

As our own Isaac Trotter explains, if Haugh can improve his range shooting, he won't have to wait long to hear his name called in the 2027 NBA Draft.

When it comes to how the talent broke down by conference, it was a a pretty level playing field for the most part.

Not to spoil anyting, but Arizona freshman Caleb Holt did not make the cut. He did, however, turn some heads in the Wildcats' exhibition game.

Loyalty is an excellent quality to have in a friend or partner. It's also why we love dogs.

It should not be quite as prevalent among college football coaches, some of whom have been undone because they did what was comfortable, not what was necessarily best for the team.

Our own John Talty highlighted five high-profile coaches who have been loyal to a fault, making hires and personnel decisions that have come back to haunt them. One of those coaches is Mike Elko. After a shaky season from Marcel Reed in 2025, Texas A&M chose not to pursue an upgrade in the portal.

Instead, the Aggies gave Reed a major payday, and they'll miss the College Football Playoff because of it.

Look, it can happen to the best of us. Dan Lanning and Dabo Swinney wound up on the list, despite the success that those two have had throughout their careers.

Steve Sarkisian is another coach who has fallen into the trap of being too loyal, but he may have a huge decision on his hands in the offseason. Arch Manning has struggled enough that another year in college should be on the table. If that happens, would Sark welcome back Manning with open arms, despite his shortcomings?

Finally, one person for whom loyalty is no an issue is Missouri QB Austin Simmons. After Trinidad Chambliss won the starting job at Ole Miss last year, Simmons didn't feel the need to stick around, but there won't be bitterness when Simmons returns to Oxford this weekend.

#2694. When Scott Boras' phone rings, agent quips: 'Just another owner begging to meet with Skubal'

LAS VEGAS (AP) — Scott Boras was 15 minutes into his annual pun-filled news conference at the general managers meetings when a cellphone rang in his pocket.

"Just another owner begging to meet with Skubal," baseball's most visible agent quipped Wednesday.

Boras represents about two dozen free agents in what Major League Baseball hopes is the last offseason without a salary cap. Tarik Skubal, a Boras client, could set a contract record for a pitcher.

Teams are negotiating to reach deals before an expected lockout starts Dec. 2.

"There's a clear intent on a group of players," said Boras, whose free agent clients include Randy Arozarena, Nick Martinez and Max Scherzer. "They're pursuing it aggressively."

MLB's five-year labor contract expires Dec. 1 at 12:59 p.m. EST and management is expected to immediately start the sport's 10th work stoppage since 1972.

On the day before the lockout began in 2021, there were 27 announced contracts that totaled more than $1.4 billion — include deals for Boras clients Corey Seager and Marcus Semien that accounted for $500 million.

Boras maintained veteran players are willing to sit out in order to fight off a cap, which owners have proposed for the first time since a 7 1/2-month strike in 1994 and '95.

"They are the ones that are the most aware," he said. "They are recipients of what others did for them and they are in great places in their lives and they're more than willing to share, contribute, aid and frankly stabilize the approach that the veterans took for them to apply to the young players of today."

He called management's proposal to increase the major league minimum salary to $900,000 a carrot.

"They're so repetitious. They are anticipated," he said. "Those are very de minimis advances, knowing the ask of what they want to take away."

He used the term "Reven-occhio" — wordplay on the children's story character Pinocchio, whose nose grows when he lies — to say MLB's claims economic change is needed are belied by private equity's investment in teams. He claimed a salary cap was "something that is going to create a true talent tyranny" and increase club equity value at a far higher rate than player salaries.

"The Broncos sell for $4.5 billion five years ago and the Seahawks sell for $9.6 billion," Boras said, citing approximate amount of those deals. "Over 100% increase in franchise value. What's the cap structure do for the players? And the reality of it is they're sitting there going with this modest increase of half that, 50%."

"The asset class of our game is documented throughout by genius owners, genius owners having the freedom, the ability under this system, to come in and advance their thoughts, to bring in the wherewithal for them to grow a franchise to its optimum," he said.

— "It's very clear that there is a dominant and strong Sku-Bull market."

— "Teams are not devoid of pursuing their championship fortunes and they understand there's only one Tarik card."

— "Teams have filled their tanks and they're all clearly ready for the Skubal dive."

#2692. The Suns need to search for another scorer alongside Booker

With the season off to a slow start, many Suns fans have expressed frustration with the team, myself included. Whether it's how the starting lineup fits, the lack of cohesion on defense, the lack of a second star, or frustration with shooting percentages, there's something for someone to pick at and be mad about. For a team that was supposed to build on last year's success, it hasn't looked that bright just yet. They have shown in spurts that they can be this solid, but ultimately their shortcomings seem to overpower their positives.

Injuries to the team's frontcourt at the start of the year forced the Suns into a situation they may not have been as prepared for, and it has ultimately cost them. Then you add Jordan Goodwin being out and missing his hustle and rebounding, and there seem to be some issues. Especially when you look at the fact that in two games, Devin Booker has dropped over 30 points and the team has lost by a landslide; in this recent game vs. the Spurs and the one last week against the Trail Blazers, Booker was on and showed he can be that number one option for this team. He can hunt his shots, find them, and, most importantly, he is not washed.

Sadly, in both of those games, Booker had no one else show up offensively to help him. This is where the main problem comes into play, as the Suns' owner, Mat Ishbia, wants to win a championship, and one with Booker at the helm. Unfortunately, when your second-highest-paid player is the same position and functions best in the same role as your 1A star, you have a problem, and that is where Jalen Green comes into play.

Now it's not all Green's fault, since they're asking him to play a role he's never played in his career, and he's not too bad at it. Yes, he turns the ball over a lot when he mishandles it, but he can make some nice passes to create plays. The problem is that since he always has to make the pass, he also wants to hunt his shot when others are out. That doesn't work for Green, though, because it forces contested looks or shots, disrupting the team's rhythm. His averages this year clearly show this: his worst in six years.

Can he be a good player? For sure, but it depends on whether he can play a role he won't succeed in on a team that needs a true playmaker and facilitator. That will not help Booker and has proven to be the case this year. Will the Suns regret trading Green, though? No, because the fit was never going to work with how they're constructed, with Booker in the same role as Green.

So how does one get this second star in Phoenix, you may ask, right? Well, that goal may be one of the bigger obstacles for this team, since they lack draft capital. Remember that 2033 pick that the Suns traded for Miles Bridges? That was the team's most valuable asset, and yet they traded it the day they could for someone who, at best, would be the third offensive option.

Your assets are either Dillon Brooks, Miles Bridges, Mark Williams, or Jalen Green. Their value isn't enough to get you anything relevant for the next step. For everyone clamoring for Kyrie Irving, Anthony Davis, and Darius Garland, those players will cost a decent amount of pick value to acquire. With Green basically looking like a glorified six-man for the Suns in his best role, how would that trade value get boosted enough for other teams to see him as a positive?

That is why, sadly, this hunt for that second star may have to wait on Khaman Maluach's development. The big man has looked solid since moving into his bench role, and with more development this year, he can truly set himself up to take those next steps toward becoming a top-tier big man. This year, it seems like the team is trying to figure out new roles for the players we have and then make a playoff run. The offseason will focus on adding a second star player and freeing up time for this big-man duo to cement themselves as the true starter and backup.

At this point, I do think waiting that long is just not going to be beneficial. At this rate, we have seen that the true "second option" cannot be that, given his new role as the point guard. Brooks has to step up, and even though he can do it, the Suns should not be living and dying by his catch-and-shoot three for this season to be impactful. In his best role as the best defender, Brooks should be the third or fourth offensive option.

The game plan for the Suns seems tough, but there may be some light at the end of the tunnel. Even though we are just around 10 games in, there are clear issues that need to be addressed before the trade deadline. Some of them are even as early as next week, but time will tell if they make those adjustments or stand pat until they can actually pivot in a direction. With all that said, though, one thing is clear: if the Suns want another chance at a championship with Booker, they need another top-tier scoring option.

Christian Mahogany will return as the Lions’ starting left guard on Sunday, a week after his benching for a violation of team rules.

Mahogany apologized to the team Wednesday morning and was back with the first-team offense in the afternoon.

#2683. Cowboys report card: Grading the first half of the season

If the first nine weeks of the regular season were like an amusement park ride for the Dallas Cowboys, they'd be bumper cars. You remember them being great as a kid, so you're excited to hop in the car and take it for another spin. It's different. Now that you're older, the mystique is gone.

The gas pedal doesn't work anymore; sometimes you don't fit in the car, and you walk out with more back pain than you've felt in your lifetime. The defense is the cool bumper car in the corner no one can seem to fix, and the offense is the bumper car that can only turn right.

After Brian Schottenheimer's first year as head coach finished with a 7-9-1 record, it feels as if the team has somehow taken a step back. In the first four weeks of the season, it looked like the offense would carry the defense to the finish line. After three horrible losses to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, Green Bay Packers, and Arizona Cardinals, the Cowboys' offense struggled to find its identity.

There have been some bright spots over nine weeks and a win over the Indianapolis Colts helps, but the report card for the first half of the season isn't filled with A-grades, despite the roster's star power.

When Quinnen Williams signed his contract extension with the Cowboys this offseason, it set the clock on whether or not the Micah Parsons trade officially pays off. It took Williams some time to find his footing in a system he hasn't played in since college, but over the last five weeks he looks like an All-Pro at defensive tackle.

Among all defensive tackles, Williams is tied for fifth in sacks (5), third in total pressures (31), and is first in tackles for loss (14). His leadership in the locker room has been praised as a big reason why the defense is starting to turn a corner. Just like his counterpart on offense, Dak Prescott, Williams will have to help carry his unit the rest of the way if they want to make a postseason push, starting Sunday vs. the 49ers.

After starting out of the gate extremely hot, CeeDee Lamb cooled off vs. the Packers, Cardinals, and Bucs. He had a dominant performance against the Philadelphia Eagles, but against those three teams, Lamb caught 18 passes for 137 yards and zero touchdowns. Then he bounced back vs. the Colts, with 10 receptions for 195 yards and a touchdown in the absence of George Pickens.

The offense needs to be more consistent with getting Lamb the ball because when he is cooking defensive backs, this team looks better overall. In four out of the five games where Lamb has scored a touchdown, Dallas has won. It's not always that simple, but in this case, it might be. His ability to bring up the entire team keeps him at an A grade for the year.

No one has surprised more this season than Tyler Guyton and his development. The Cowboys have put all their faith in Guyton and never gave up on him, and it's paid off. Guyton might not be a Pro Bowl player yet, but he's looked better than he has in the last two years at left tackle and, more importantly, has stayed healthy.

Coming into the year, he was the team's biggest question mark. Now he's turned into one of the team's most consistent players up front.

Like Lamb, Joey Porter Jr. has been able to raise all boats when he's been healthy and on the field.

The biggest disappointment of Porter's tenure so far in Dallas is that he hasn't been fully healthy and has been bouncing between the field and the sideline. That's why this grade is more on a curve of what he can be. He rolled his ankle in practice a few weeks ago, and he doesn't seem 100 percent healthy, considering he only played 36 snaps on defense vs. the Cardinals and missed the Colts game. Christian Parker has shown he likes to rotate his cornerbacks, but JPJ needs to be on the field for almost every snap when healthy because of his impact.

The Cowboys don't have their bye week until Week 14, so they may have to manage him until then, but he's been an All-Pro-level corner when he locks down wide receivers for Dallas.

There have certainly been A+ moments for the Cowboys quarterback, but overall, Dak Prescott has been very good this season—not elite. His inability to find answers against the blitz, which he's normally great at, hurts him here.

Prescott was phenomenal in the second half of the Houston Texans game and in the Philadelphia Eagles matchup, but given what those teams have turned into, it wasn't high-level competition. Prescott is currently third among quarterbacks in passing yards (2,381), tied for seventh in touchdown passes (16), and is third in quarterback rating (77.0).

The second half of the season will define his 2026 campaign more as he tries to dig Dallas out of the playoff hole they're in right now. He'll have to do it against big-time competition in the San Francisco 49ers, Jacksonville Jaguars, and Seattle Seahawks.

Just when the pro personnel department looks like its decision-making needs to be questioned, they find a diamond in the rough like Otito Ogbonnia. The Cowboys defensive tackle has been a force in stopping the run. Ogbonnia leads all defensive linemen with 18 run stops, per Pro Football Focus. Prior to joining Dallas, Ogbonnia never had more than 12 stops in a season.

He's only here on a one-year deal, but the Cowboys need to find a way to re-sign him to a long-term contract because he's shown he's worthy of it, and he complements what Dallas wants to do up front with their defensive tackle rotation.

The Cowboys bell cow picked up right where he left off a season ago. After having a career year in Dallas, Javonte Williams looks poised to repeat the same success that earned him a contract extension this offseason. Williams sits ninth in rushing yards for the year (629), averaging 4.1 yards per carry, and is tied for second in rushing touchdowns (9).

While the Cowboys were trying to find their identity in the run game, there were a few times Williams didn't seem to see the holes well or couldn't bounce the ball outside. He's never going to be Bijan Robinson or Jahmyr Gibbs, but he can be the best back Dallas needs when they are trying to establish the run. Look no further than his career performance vs. the Eagles when he rushed for 155 yards off 25 carries.

Caleb Downs' and Jaishawn Barham's performance vs. the Baltimore Ravens is doing the heavy lifting for the overall grade of Dallas' top three draft picks. Downs has had to rotate from nickel corner to safety a few times this season while the defense dealt with injuries in the secondary. That's a lot for a rookie—even one with his football intelligence—to process. That's why at times Downs has looked like a fish out of water. However, his game vs. the Colts is exactly what the Cowboys hoped for when drafting him and what they're hoping to see the rest of the season.

As for Barham and first-round pick Malachi Lawrence, there have been moments, but largely inconsistent. With DeMarvion Overshown coming back healthy, Barham is back on the bench, where it might be better for him to take some time and learn more from his peers. As a downhill defender in the run game, Barham has shown to have high-level instincts and a feel for finding the ball carrier. But in the passing game, he's looked lost and slow, which makes him a liability on third down.

Lawrence may be done for the season, going on injured reserve after the Arizona Cardinals game. The hope is that he will return for the year, but depending on what the next three weeks look like, Dallas may decide to shut him down for 2026 and look toward 2027. This year was all about getting the reps at the NFL level, so it's disappointing to see him put on the shelf for critical moments in his development. Prior to the injury, Lawrence was starting to stack some good weeks.

The Cowboys' right tackle has been very average so far, which is actually a win considering what we've seen in the past. Terence Steele hasn't been Lane Johnson, but he also hasn't been Chaz Green this year. His pass blocking has improved, allowing only three sacks, which is near a career low for him. Before his knee injury, Steele was known to be a mauler in the run game. That hasn't shown up as much this year, considering Dallas' run success has come when they go behind Tyler Guyton and Tyler Smith.

If Steele can stay at a C+ grade for the rest of the season, then there shouldn't be any reason why Prescott isn't finding his receivers and going through his progressions. I'm sure most coaches around the league would take average play from their tackles as long as they don't get beat.

The curious case of George Pickens. Was he ever going to repeat the All-Pro version of himself we saw in 2025? Probably not with a healthy CeeDee Lamb in the lineup. But up to this point, Pickens has disappointed given the expectations before the season. To tell you the truth, it's not his fault either.

Yes, he could be a better blocker in the run game, but there shouldn't be a game where Brevyn Spann-Ford has more targets in the passing attack than Pickens. Brian Schottenheimer has to do a better job of manufacturing touches for Pickens. Similar to his counterpart in Lamb, when Pickens gets rolling, he's virtually unstoppable.

Just look at what Ja'Marr Chase and Tee Higgins are doing in Cincinnati with the Bengals. Cowboys fans can only hope the second half of the season looks more like that for the duo in Dallas.

With the arrival of Quinnen Williams last year, a lot of the pressure came off Kenny Clark to be "that dude" on the interior of the D-line. Having him and Williams together as a tandem was set up to be the best defensive tackle duo Dallas has ever had. Like many players in this grade range, there have been moments when it looks like Clark can turn back the clock to his old self, but he also looks like a player past his prime who can't consistently play the way he's supposed to.

At 31, Clark is on track to have the lowest PFF grade of his career: 57.4. He's been generating pressures and is above league average with 20 among starting defensive tackles, but it's not good enough given the expectations around him coming into the year. He's a great leader in the locker room and will be great for a player like LT Overton, but for now, Clark has been okay through the first half of the season.

Taking Malachi Lawrence out of the mix, the most disappointing thing about the Cowboys this season has been their inability to get sacks or production from their outside linebackers. Donovan Ezeiruaku, Rashan Gary, and Von Miller have provided no juice when rushing the quarterback. Most of their sacks this year, which isn't many to begin with, have come when Williams pressures the middle or when they get coverage sacks.

Ezeiruaku was supposed to take a huge step forward in year two and get close to the pass-rushing production he had at Boston College. Only 2.5 sacks at this point in the year is not what the Cowboys were hoping for. Miller was supposed to roll out of bed and get eight sacks. He's only recorded one sack through nine games.

Then there's Rashan Gary. He is on the leadership council and is consistently showing up on the Cowboys Sounds from the Sidelines, hyping up defenders around him, which is great. The running game has been a disaster, and he hasn't been able to set the edge. He might not be the same pass rusher he once was, but when Gary arrived in Dallas, the expectation was that he could replace what the defense was missing when DeMarcus Lawrence left.

If it wasn't for Malachi Lawrence's injury, the coaching staff would have to think hard about making Gary a rotation player and giving the rookie more snaps. Unfortunately, Dallas needs Gary to be a starter, considering there's no one else, and Miller is a liability in the running game too.

With BT Jordan in the building as a pass-rush specialist, the hope was that he could get these guys to perform at a high level, as he has with the Broncos in Denver. With seven of Dallas' 17 total sacks this year coming from their outside linebackers, it's not the coaching that's poor; it might be a lack of talent at the position.

#2679. Connor Hellebuyck trade: Jets send star goalie to the Devils in exchange for four players, two draft picks

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Connor Hellebuyck is a now a Devil. The star goalie for the Winnipeg Jets is on the move after being traded to New Jersey on Friday in exchange for four players and two future draft picks. the teams announced the move with the Jets receiving Dawson Mercer, Nick Bjugstad, Nico Daws and Alexander Command, plus a 2027 seventh-round pick and a 2029 second-round pick.

Hellebuyck expressed his desire to be traded in the offseason when he formally requested a move in August. He said at the time that he had made the request months earlier and tried to keep the situation private.

Hellebuyck has spent his entire career with Winnipeg after being drafted by the Jets in 2012 at No. 130 overall. He's recognized as one of the best goalies in the league as a three-time Vezina Trophy winner. He also helped carry the United States to its first gold medal since 1980 at the 2026 Olympics in February with some incredible saves against Canada in the final game.

After trading Jacob Markstom in the offseason, the Devils had a clear need in goal, and this splashy move certainly fills that need. With a talented young core already in place, New Jersey's Stanley Cup window is wide open.

RAISE HELLE!Connor Hellebuyck is a New Jersey Devil: https://t.co/HCehRGOQI5 pic.twitter.com/dZGNQR16m1

For the Jets, it must be a hard pill to swallow when a franchise icon decides to walk out they door, but this trade package should help them as the enter a new era and revamp the roster. Winnipeg got a former first-rounder in Mercer to try and add to a rebuild as well as a veteran presence in Bjugstad. They also acquired a younger goalie in Daws who could fill the role of Hellebuyck at just 25 years old.

Goaltending has been an issue in New Jersey for a while now -- even after the team acquired Markstrom from the Calgary Flames in 2024. Markstom never really panned out, and his 13.6 goals allowed above average, per Natural Stat Trick, were a big reason why the Devils missed the postseason last year.

In the early portion of this season, it was clear that New Jersey needed to make a move to upgrade in the crease. Daws and veteran Jake Allen simply aren't a tandem suitable for a Stanley Cup contender, and the numbers backed that up. New Jersey ranks 24th in team save percentage at .877, and the duo of Daws and Allen combined to surrender 2.99 goals above average.

Once Hellebuyck gets up to game speed, that shouldn't be a problem anymore.

In the three-season stretch from 2023-26, Hellebuyck led the NHL with 73.42 goals saved above average, which is 20 goals higher than the next closest netminder. Over that span, Hellebuyck also posted a standard save percentage of .914 and an astronomical high-danger save-percentage of .832.

Hellebuyck carried less talented teams to the playoffs multiple times in his career. Now on a team loaded with weaponry in their prime -- Jack Hughes, Jesper Bratt and Nico Hischier to name a few -- Hellebuyck could be the final piece to the championship puzzle.

In terms of the acquisition cost, it was probably an easy deal for Devils general manager Sunny Mehta to make. The 2029 second-round pick is useless for a team that should be all-in now, Bjugstad is simply a depth piece and Daws now has no path to a starting role with Hellebuyck in town.

The most interesting trade chips are Mercer and Command. Mercer flashed major upside with 56 points in his second NHL season, 2022-23, but he hasn't really come close to hitting those heights again. Still, even if he has plateaued, Mercer remains a strong middle-six forward rising into his prime.

Although Command had his detractors -- and may have been over-drafted at No. 12 overall -- he was a consensus first-round pick last summer. That gives Winnipeg a potential franchise forward it can build around long-term, but New Jersey already has one of the deepest forward groups in the league, especially with the emergence of Arseny Gritsyuk and the acquisition of Luke Evangelista.

If we're looking for a 3-D chess angle of this deal, it only makes the Devils more appealing for a certain Minnesota Wild defenseman whose brothers just happen to play in New Jersey already. Grade -- A+

Let's get the obvious out of the way first: The Jets were never going to get fair value for Hellebuyck because, at his best, he's the No. 1 goaltender in the world with no equal. That type of excellence can't be replaced.

That said, Winnipeg did fairly well given the circumstances. Hellebuyck made a public trade request, and he wasn't even with the team after sitting out for the entirety of training camp. The entire league knew the Jets had to trade him.

Hellebuyck's talent created a decent market anyway, but most of the suitors were bona fide Stanley Cup contenders with little in the way of valuable draft capital, and they weren't going to knee cap the roster by sending a key player back in return.

With all that taken into consideration, Kevin Cheveldayoff got a solid return. Although Mercer's ceiling may be lower than initially thought, he's a 24-year-old forward who banks roughly 20 goals and 20 assists every season. The kicker with Mercer will be Winnipeg's ability to re-sign him before he hits restricted free agency next summer.

The addition of Command means Winnipeg now has two forwards selected in the top 12 of the 2026 NHL Draft after taking center Viggo Bjorck themselves. If both of those players deliver on their first-round pedigrees, they could be a terrific one-two punch for the team long-term.

Daws was a third-round pick in 2020, and despite playing just 13 NHL games since the start of the 2024-25 season, he should give Winnipeg a solid back up option behind Stuart Skinner. It certainly helps that Skinner is off to a great start with his new team -- and if Daws develops into a true No. 1 -- it'll be gravy.

If there's any reason to critique this deal from the Jets' side of things, it's that they didn't get premium draft capital or a surefire up-and-coming prospect. Maybe Command develops into a star, but there's no guarantee he becomes a top-six stud in the NHL.

The Jets got a lot of good stuff, but they didn't really get anything great, at least not based on what we know in the moment. Because of that, I have to ding Winnipeg a little bit. Grade: B

#2678. 'It's forever': Lakers rookie Cameron Carr cherishing first NBA points

The son of former NBA dunk contest runner-up Chris Carr, Lakers rookie Cameron Carr envisioned his first NBA points coming on a lob. When asked before the draft in April, the first-round pick knew that if not on a sky-high alley-oop his first bucket would at least be something athletic.

He now gives himself half-credit for calling his shot.

The 21-year-old Lakers guard scored his first NBA points on a fastbreak dunk Monday in Atlanta, making the most of his opportunities during the Lakers' hot start.

Carr had two points and three rebounds in seven minutes and 19 seconds in the Lakers' win over the Atlanta Hawks in the first significant playing time of his professional career. The Lakers, who finish a three-game, four-day road trip in Milwaukee on Wednesday, have the top record in the NBA at 10-2 with a six-game winning streak.

Carr helped extend the Lakers' streak by bolstering a shorthanded lineup against the Hawks. The Lakers needed the rookie Monday when they were without Austin Reaves (illness) and Quentin Grimes (right finger sprain).

Three weeks into his NBA career, Carr, the 24th overall pick the Lakers traded up to acquire from the New York Knicks, said he is still nervous any time he subs into a game. Getting the first of what he hopes will be many NBA points helped settle his nerves.

Read more: What we've learned about the first-place Lakers

"Over time it's only going to grow, it's only going to get better," Carr said. "I'm only going to get more and more confident, so every time I get a chance to step out there, just show what I can do and of course show my talents through God's work."

The 6-foot-5 guard is a skilled scorer and an athletic marvel. He couldn't even touch the rim when, one summer, he begged his father, who was the runner-up in the 1997 dunk contest to Kobe Bryant, to teach him to dunk. He just needed one summer to master it. Carr set a single-season sophomore scoring record at Baylor last season and his 642 points rank fifth in program history regardless of class. An efficient shooter (37.4% from three in his final college season), Carr also led Baylor with 45 blocked shots.

Now in the NBA, defense is still where Carr can improve most, Lakers coach JJ Redick said. Although Carr is a talented offensive player, it is still difficult for young players to find their rhythm with limited playing time, Redick said. The Lakers staff has encouraged Carr to take advantage of stay-ready games against coaches and make the most of G League opportunities to get more reps. Carr had 13 points and four rebounds during the Coachella Valley Lakers' season opener on Friday.

"Just being patient, man," Carr said of his approach to the beginning of the season, "just putting my head down, working every day, knowing that I can be the best person I can be. And when my time, my name is called, just be ready."

Carr subbed into Monday's game with 3:35 remaining in the first quarter. The Lakers, trailing by two, soon flipped the game with 13 unanswered points to end the quarter. A steal by Luka Doncic with 1:44 remaining fueled the streak and the star point guard threw an outlet pass to Carr in transition, who collected the ball for an emphatic two-handed dunk.

Doncic dished out another assist after the game when he rushed to secure the game ball for Carr. The superstar said he wanted the rookie to remember his first NBA bucket.

"That's big time," Carr said Wednesday of Doncic's kind gesture. "Especially coming from him, that says a lot about who he is as a person and how he views this team."

Redick handed the game ball to Carr in the locker room after the win as teammates cheered. Carr broke the team huddle on the word "together." He plans to have everyone sign the ball before keeping it in a trophy case.

"There's no price on it," Carr said. "It's forever."

The Lakers swapped out two-way centers Tuesday, waiving Lawson Lovering and signing Carson Cooper, the team announced. Both previously played in the Memphis Grizzlies organization and Cooper made one NBA appearance for the Grizzlies after signing a two-way deal with the team.

Cooper didn't become a regular starter in college until his senior season, when he started all 35 games for Michigan State. The four-year Spartan averaged 11.1 points on 58.4% shooting with 7.1 rebounds, 1.5 assists and one block in his final season.

Lovering, who signed a two-way deal with the Lakers on Oct. 28, appeared in Lakers blowouts against Miami and Sacramento with a rebound and a block.

#2677. Treydan Stukes provides silver lining in Las Vegas Raiders’ Week 9 blowout loss to San Francisco 49ers

The Las Vegas Raiders' defense is searching for answers after giving up 30 or more points for the sixth consecutive game in the Week 9 loss to the San Francisco 49ers. However, the Raiders might have found at least one solution with rookie safety Treydan Stukes.

Stukes has been playing well and getting better just about every week, and last Sunday in San Francisco was his best performance to date. The former Arizona Wildcat nabbed his second career interception (first since the season opener) and yielded just 19 yards on five targets (four catches) while coming up with a couple of 'defensive stops' in coverage, according to Pro Football Focus. That was good enough to earn PFF's fifth-highest coverage grade (85.8) among safeties for the week.

While there's plenty to be negative about when it comes to the Raiders' defense, let's focus on one of the few positives and break down the second-round pick's outing.

As the numbers above indicate, Stukes' impact was primarily in coverage against the 49ers. But the clip against the run above caught my eye.

San Francisco comes out in 22 personnel with fullback Kyle Juszczyk as one of three strong-side tight ends initially. That's how Kyle Shanahan likes to run 13 personnel plays/formations while keeping Juszczyk on the field. Meanwhile, the Raiders had the rookie safety cover George Kittle frequently throughout the game, so he's on the line of scrimmage and on the strong side of the formation.

When Juszczyk motions to the weak-side pre-snap, linebacker Quay Walker signals for Stukes to stay inside so that Stukes can cover Kittle with inside leverage if it's a pass play. The problem with that is it puts a defensive back in the C-gap, where he's in future Hall of Fame left tackle Trent Williams' path if the 49ers run outside zone, which is exactly what Shanahan dials up.

That's a mismatch in the offense's favor since a safety is taking on a block from one of (if not the) best offensive tackles in the game. However, the rookie doesn't back down.

Stukes eyes Kittle initially, and once he reads run, he redirects to take on Williams' block and ends up resetting the line of scrimmage by winning at the point of attack. That helps force running back Christian McCaffrey to cut upfield and right into linebacker Tommy Eichenberg for a short gain.

While Stukes doesn't make the tackle here, he makes the play by beating a high-quality opponent in a disadvantageous matchup to force the running back to redirect into an unblocked defender. That's pretty impressive run support from a defensive back.

But again, the safety's impact was felt the most in the passing game. While the interception was undoubtedly the best play he made on the afternoon (don't worry, that play is coming later), Stukes made a handful of quality tackles that kept San Francisco behind the sticks.

Here, it's second and 20, and the Raiders line up in a two-high look pre-snap before rolling a safety down into the curl-to-flat area and running Cover 3 post-snap. Stukes is the safety spinning into the second level, and he shows some situational awareness by staying deep in his area. That does two things: it makes it more difficult to throw a pass over his head and influences the quarterback to make a short throw.

Thus, Brock Purdy throws the quick out route to the slot receiver, which is what the Raiders want him to do in this situation. That's where Stukes' closing speed comes in, as he rallies to the football and makes a nice open-field tackle to limit the yards after the catch. Now, San Francisco faces 3rd and 15. Just don't ask what happens on the next play…(Purdy scrambles for 18 yards).

This time, Las Vegas starts in a one-high look and rotates into Cover 2. Stukes, playing nickelback, lines up over Kittle and is responsible for the hook-to-curl area of the coverage. Initially, the safety reads the tight end and sees the tight end chip block before releasing into a flat route, taking Kittle out of Stukes' area/assignment. So, the rookie shifts his eyes to the backfield and starts looking for a crossing route from the other side of the field.

Meanwhile, the 49ers have their outside receiver in the trips formation at the bottom of the screen run a drag route into Stukes' area. He sees that, parks himself at the sticks and pounces once Purdy lets the ball go. That's where the closing speed comes in, again, as he makes the tackle just short of the sticks to put the offense in a fourth-and-short situation. That set up one of the Raiders' few stops last Sunday.

Technically, this play is still a positive result for the offense since San Francisco gets five yards on first and 10 to stay on schedule. But considering the rookie safety's assignment, this is still an impressive rep.

He lines up as a deep safety in a two-high look pre-snap but is in man coverage with the tight end, Kittle. Meanwhile, the 49ers run an RPO where Kittle is on a flat route against not just off coverage, but a safety playing over 10 yards off the ball. That makes Purdy's decision easy, as he aborts the run play and just dumps the ball into the flat.

In theory, the tight end should have enough room to pick up the first down or at least set up the offense in a second-and-short situation. However, Stukes' closing speed allows him to make contact right at the line of scrimmage despite how deep he was playing.

Now, the tackle can be better since he does allow too many yards after contact. But Kittle is one of the hardest tight ends in the NFL to bring down, so there's no shame in that. Plus, the defense still has a decent chance to get off the field in a second-and-five situation.

Now, the moment you all have been waiting for: the aforementioned interception! What really makes this rep impressive is that the first-year pro makes a play where he shows the awareness or football IQ of a well-tenured veteran.

As we've seen on a handful of occasions already, Stukes starts in two-high and spins down into a Cover 3 look. Granted, the play call is a little different, where Taron Johnson blitzes off the edge for a three-deep, three-under fire zone. That means the safety essentially takes over the nickel's coverage assignment by picking up the slot receiver, who is running a return route (out and then in).

Stukes' eyes are the big key here. He's staring in the backfield throughout the rep, using his peripheral vision to read the receiver's route and match the receiver's movement patterns step for step. So when Purdy rears back to throw, the rookie safety is able to read the quarterback's eyes, come off his man and sink on the drag route from the other side of the field to climb the ladder and pick the pass off.

This is what happens when instincts meet athleticism, as that was one hell of a catch too. Well done, rook, well done!

#2676. Browns WR Denzel Boston is expected back at practice Thursday

The Browns practiced without wide receiver Denzel Boston on Wednesday, but they don’t expect his absence to be an extended one.

Boston is listed with a toe injury and head coach Todd Monken said at his pre-practice press conference that the second-round pick is expected to be back on the field on Thursday.

#2674. How Martina Navratilova once won the WTA Finals twice in the same year

The event, hosted in Boca Raton, Florida, was won by 18-time major champion Chris Evert, who defeated Australian player Kerry Melville in the final.

Since then, the likes of Steffi Graf, Monica Seles and Serena Williams have all won the prestigious end-of-year event.

With eight singles titles to her name, Martina Navratilova is the most successful player in tournament history.

Remarkably, in 1986, the Czech-American star managed to win the singles event on two occasions.

Between 1972 and 1974, the WTA Finals were held in October. The Tour then moved the event to March from 1975 to 1986.

In 1986, the WTA decided to shift to a January to November season, resulting in the WTA Finals – then named the Virginia Slims Championships – being moved from March to November.

As a result, the Australian Open – which was previously held in December – did not take place, and the WTA Finals were held twice: in March and November.

Martina Navratilova won both events, beating Hana Mandlikova and Steffi Graf in the respective finals. Navratilova was the number one seed at both events.

"Once I was up by two sets, I felt comfortable," Navratilova said after defeating Graf 7–6, 6–3, 6–2 in the November final. "I played a solid match, nothing spectacular, but no letdowns. This win was fantastic."

"I'm playing against tougher competition, and that's what makes it more gratifying," she added. "I've had to play as good, if not better, than two years ago."

Navratilova also reached the final in 1989, 1991 and 1992, but lost to Steffi Graf in 1989 and Monica Seles in 1991 and 1992.

1986 – defeated Evonne Goolagong Cawley in the final, 7-6, 6-4

1979 – defeated Tracy Austin in the final, 6–3, 3–6, 6–2

1981 – defeated Andrea Jaeger in the final, 6–3, 7–6

1983 – defeated Chris Evert in the final, 6-2, 6-0

1983 – defeated Chris Evert in the final, 6–3, 7–5, 6–1

1984 – defeated Helen Sukova in the final, 6–3, 7–5, 6–4

1986 [March]: defeated Hana Mandlikova in the final, 6–2, 6–0, 3–6, 6–1

1989 [November]: defeated Steffi Graf in the final, 7–6, 6–3, 6–2

Navratilova also won 13 WTA Finals doubles titles, which is also a record. She won her last title at the event in 1991 alongside Pam Shriver.
